items.prompt: While scanning an array, the current prefix sum is s. To count subarrays ending at the current index whose sum is exactly k, which prior prefix value must be matched?
constraints: Prefix sums are taken before and through the current position under one consistent convention.
The array may contain negative values.

options.text: A prior prefix equal to s - k.
A prior prefix equal to s + k.
Any prior prefix equal to k, regardless of s.
Only a prior prefix equal to the current s.

feedback.reason: If currentPrefix - priorPrefix = k, then priorPrefix must equal currentPrefix - k.

blocks.text: A subarray sum is the difference between two prefix states. Rearranging s - p = k gives p = s - k, so a frequency map can report how many valid starts exist for the current end. The rule does not require sorted or nonnegative values; it relies only on algebraic cancellation and on querying prior state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.s_plus_k: This would make s - priorPrefix = -k, not k. The sign follows directly from rearranging the range-difference equation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.k_only: The required prior state changes with the current prefix s. A fixed lookup of k ignores where the current scan has accumulated to.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.current_s: Matching s counts zero-sum subarrays, because s - s = 0. It is correct only when k = 0.

items.prompt: To count all subarrays with sum k, what should the hash map store for each prefix value?
constraints: Different start boundaries may have the same prefix value.
The output is a count, not one example subarray.

options.text: Only the most recent index where the prefix value occurred.
The number of prior boundaries that produced that prefix value.
The sorted list of input values seen so far.
The length of the current moving window.

feedback.reason: Every prior occurrence of s - k defines a distinct valid start boundary, so multiplicity is part of the answer.

blocks.text: When the current prefix is s, the answer increases by frequency[s - k]. Storing only one index can find one candidate but loses other starts with the same cumulative value. The map represents historical boundary multiplicity, not a moving window or a sorted value summary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_index_only: A last-index map is sufficient for some existence or longest-length variants, but it undercounts when multiple prior boundaries have the required value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_values: Sorting values loses the prefix-by-position relation. The needed key is a cumulative boundary value, and the needed payload is its count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.current_window_length: Negative values can make valid starts non-monotonic, so one current window does not enumerate all subarrays ending here.

items.prompt: Order the operations for counting subarrays with sum k during one left-to-right prefix-hash scan.
constraints: The frequency map contains only prefix boundaries that occur before the current boundary when the lookup happens.
Score is based on preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Initialize frequency[0] = 1 for the empty prefix.
Add the current array value to the running prefix s.
Read frequency[s - k] and add it to the answer.
Advance to the next array position.

feedback.reason: The lookup must see prior boundaries but not count the current boundary as its own earlier start.

blocks.text: Each prefix state belongs to an array boundary. The map must contain only boundaries earlier than the current one when the scan counts a nonempty subarray ending here.

items: Before scanning, seed frequency[0] = 1 for the single boundary before index 0.
Add the current array value to s, moving s to the boundary after that element.
Add frequency[s - k] to the answer; each stored occurrence is an earlier start boundary whose difference from s is k.
Increment frequency[s] only after counting, making the current boundary available to later ends.
Advance to the next position and repeat.

blocks.title: Lookup must precede insertion
blocks.text: If k = 0 and frequency[s] is incremented first, the lookup can pair the current boundary with itself and count an empty interval. Lookup-before-insert preserves the nonempty-subarray contract.

items.prompt: Why must frequency[0] start at 1 before scanning when counting subarrays with sum k?
constraints: The running prefix before reading any element is 0.

options.text: It prevents the running prefix from becoming negative.
It makes hash-map iteration sorted by key.
It represents the one boundary before index 0, allowing a current prefix equal to k to count a subarray starting at 0.
It lets the algorithm run without storing any other prefix values.

feedback.reason: The empty prefix is a real start boundary with cumulative value zero.

blocks.text: If s = k at index r, then the required prior prefix is s - k = 0. The seeded occurrence corresponds to the boundary before A[0], so the subarray [0, r] is counted uniformly. Omitting the seed forces a special case and misses these ranges; adding it does not control signs, ordering, or storage size.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.avoid_negative_prefixes: The running sum may legitimately be negative. The seed exists for boundary completeness, not monotonicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_hash_keys: A hash map does not become sorted because one key is initialized. Lookup order is irrelevant to correctness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.remove_extra_space: The algorithm still stores frequencies for potentially O(n) distinct prefix values. One seed does not eliminate auxiliary state.

items.prompt: Why is prefix sum plus hash frequency suitable for counting exact-sum subarrays when A may contain negative values?
constraints: All subarrays with sum k must be counted.
No sorting or reordering is permitted.

options.text: The hash map converts every negative value into a positive value.
It is simply a moving window stored in a hash table.
It first sorts the array so all negative values appear before positive values.
It matches the required prior cumulative value even when the running sum rises and falls, so no monotonic shrink rule is needed.

feedback.reason: The lookup equation works over non-monotonic cumulative history; it does not depend on a one-direction window repair rule.

blocks.text: With negative values, increasing the right boundary can increase or decrease the sum, so a simple “shrink while too large” window can miss solutions. Prefix-hash matching asks only whether prior s - k states exist, preserving every legal start boundary. It remains a prefix-history method, not a window hidden inside a map.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negatives_become_positive: Hashing does not change values. Correctness comes from exact key equality on cumulative sums, including negative keys.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_and_prefix_same: A window maintains one current interval and moves its boundaries. Prefix-hash state retains many prior boundaries simultaneously.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_then_hash: Sorting destroys subarray contiguity and is unnecessary. The scan must follow original order.

items.prompt: A developer sorts A before running the prefix-hash algorithm for subarray sum k. Why is that invalid?
constraints: A subarray means a contiguous segment of the original sequence.

options.text: Sorting changes which values are adjacent, so prefix differences describe subarrays of a different sequence.
Hash maps require insertion keys in descending order.
The running prefix must be increasing, and sorting cannot guarantee that with duplicates.
Sorting prevents storing a frequency for the same key twice.

feedback.reason: The prefix-hash equation is positional; reordering changes the set of contiguous segments being counted.

blocks.text: The algorithm works on the original scan because each pair of prefix boundaries identifies one original subarray. Sorting creates new adjacencies and therefore a different family of boundary pairs. Hash keys may arrive in any order, and prefix sums need not increase.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hash_requires_order: Hash lookup has no sorted insertion requirement. Arbitrary cumulative values are valid keys.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_must_increase: Prefixes can rise, fall, or repeat. The matching equation uses equality, not monotonicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.frequency_lost: A frequency map explicitly supports repeated keys. Sorting does not prevent repetition; it changes the sequence semantics.

items.prompt: Select the expected time and worst-case extra space for one prefix-hash scan that counts subarrays with sum k.
constraints: Hash lookup and update are expected O(1).
Up to n + 1 distinct prefix sums may occur.
The input array is not counted as extra space.

feedback.reason: The scan performs expected constant hash work per element and may retain a distinct frequency entry for every prefix boundary.

blocks.text: There are n iterations. Each performs one required-prior lookup and one current-prefix update, both expected O(1) under the stated hash-table assumption, so summing the per-element work gives expected O(n) time. In the worst case all n + 1 prefix values are distinct, so the frequency map stores O(n) entries and uses O(n) extra space.

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: Expected time is not O(1) or O(log n) because all n elements are scanned, and it is not O(n^2) because no earlier boundary is rescanned inside an iteration. Space is not O(1) or O(log n) because the map can retain one distinct key per boundary, and it is not O(n^2) because at most n + 1 boundaries—and therefore at most n + 1 distinct prefix keys—exist.

items.prompt: Which problem transfers the required-prior-prefix idea by storing a normalized prefix state instead of the raw sum?
constraints: Subarrays are contiguous in the original order.
All qualifying subarrays must be counted.

options.text: Answer range minima by subtracting two prefix remainders.
Count subarrays whose sum is divisible by m by matching equal normalized prefix remainders.
Maintain the sorted order of values by hashing each prefix sum.
Find the maximum fixed-size window by matching equal prefix frequencies only.

feedback.reason: Two prefixes with the same remainder modulo m differ by a multiple of m, so equality of normalized states is the match condition.

blocks.text: Let p and s be an earlier and current prefix sum. Their subarray difference s - p is divisible by positive m exactly when s and p have the same remainder modulo m. Store the frequency of each normalized remainder, and add the frequency matching the current one. When a language's `%` may return a negative remainder, normalize with `((prefix % m) + m) % m`, which always lies in [0, m). Range minimum has no inverse, online sorting is not a contiguous-range aggregate, and a fixed-size maximum is governed by window movement rather than frequency matching.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_minimum: Equal or subtractable remainders do not encode minima. Minimum is not derived from a pair of scalar cumulative states.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.online_sorting: Hashing prefix sums does not maintain value order. This is neither a sorting contract nor a contiguous-subarray condition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_window_max: A fixed-size maximum can be maintained by adding the entering value and removing the leaving value. Prefix-frequency equality is not the decision rule.

items.prompt: When counting subarrays with sum k using prefix frequencies, why is the current prefix queried before it is inserted into the frequency map?

options.text: It prevents the current prefix from pairing with itself and falsely counting an empty subarray.
Insertion would make the map too large to use for negative values.
The query must see prefixes in sorted order before insertion.
It removes all zero-sum subarrays from the answer.

feedback.reason: For current prefix p, a prior prefix p-k identifies a non-empty subarray ending here; inserting p first could make the zero-length pair appear when k=0.

blocks.text: The correct order is: look up prefix-k, add its frequency to the answer, then increment the frequency of prefix. Seed frequency[0]=1 before scanning to represent subarrays beginning at index zero.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.save_memory: The map stores frequencies regardless of insertion order and may need all prior prefixes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_keys: Hash lookup does not require sorted keys.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.avoid_zero_sum: Zero-sum non-empty subarrays remain countable through earlier equal prefixes.

items.prompt: Why does the subarray-counting variant store a frequency for each prefix sum instead of only its latest index?

options.text: Every earlier occurrence of prefix-k creates a distinct subarray ending at the current position.
Only the earliest prefix occurrence can form a valid subarray.
Keeping one index ensures equal prefix sums are never considered twice.
A frequency map stores the original array values for reconstruction.

feedback.reason: The output is a count, so repeated qualifying start boundaries contribute repeatedly.

blocks.text: If prefix-k has frequency three before the current prefix, there are three distinct start positions that produce sum k subarrays ending here. A latest-index map would undercount them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.need_earliest_only: Earliest occurrence is useful for maximizing length, not for counting all occurrences.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.avoid_duplicates: Those equal-prefix occurrences represent different subarray boundaries and must not be collapsed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recover_values: The map stores derived prefix-state counts, not input payloads.

items.prompt: For a current prefix sum p and target subarray sum k, which prior prefix value should a count map query?

options.text: p-k, because p - prior = k.
p+k, regardless of subarray direction.
k-p, reversing the prefix relation.
p², because prefix values are cumulative.

feedback.reason: A prior boundary p-k leaves a difference of k to the current boundary p.

blocks.text: The map stores frequencies of earlier prefixes. Add the matching frequency to the answer before inserting the current prefix.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.p_plus_k: It would make prior-current equal -k under the usual subtraction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.k_minus_p: The required prior boundary is derived by rearranging p-prior=k.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.p_squared: Squaring is unrelated to the subarray-sum relation.

items.prompt: Why is prefix frequency of zero initialized to one before scanning an array?

options.text: It represents the empty prefix before index zero, enabling subarrays that begin at zero.
It counts one input zero even when the first value is nonzero.
It keeps all prefix sums nonnegative.
It represents a prefix after the final element.

feedback.reason: The empty prefix boundary is a valid prior state for a subarray starting at the first element.

blocks.text: If current prefix equals k, querying prefix-k=0 finds that initial boundary and counts the range [0,current].

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_value_count: The seed is a boundary state, not an input occurrence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.end_boundary: The seed is before scanning, not after the input.

items.prompt: Why can prefix-hash counting handle negative array values when a positive-only window rule cannot?

options.text: It matches exact prior-prefix differences without assuming sums change monotonically as boundaries move.
It sorts negative values before inserting them.
It drops negative values from the prefix.
It relies on a window that always grows when the sum is small.

feedback.reason: Hash state tests an algebraic equality rather than a monotone window predicate.

blocks.text: Each current prefix looks up every earlier boundary that would leave target k. Signs do not change that identity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_values: Prefix order must follow original positions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_negatives: Negative contributions are part of exact sums.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_grows: That is a monotonic-window assumption, not hash-prefix matching.

items.prompt: What changes when a prefix-hash task asks for the number of matching subarrays rather than the longest one?

options.text: Store the frequency of each prior prefix so every matching start contributes.
Keep only one prior index because all matching starts are equivalent for counting.
Sort prefix values and discard their scan order.
Clear the map after every current prefix.

feedback.reason: Counting includes every earlier occurrence of the required prefix, while longest-length objectives use an index policy instead.

blocks.text: Map payload semantics follow the objective: frequency for count, earliest index for longest, or another explicitly justified witness policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_one_only: One index undercounts repeated qualifying starts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_prefixes: Sorting destroys the temporal boundary order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clear_each_step: Earlier prefixes are exactly the candidates the current prefix must match.
